name: Physics
areas: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Motion in two dimensions
Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity

points.title: Aims, questions, hypotheses and predictions
points.detail: Constructing an aim and a research question; identifying the independent, dependent and controlled variables; writing a hypothesis that can actually be tested; predicting possible outcomes.

questions.q: A student investigates how the drop height of a ball affects its rebound height. Write a testable hypothesis and identify the independent and dependent variables.
answer: Hypothesis: as the drop height increases, the rebound height will increase proportionally.
Independent variable: drop height.
Dependent variable: rebound height.
A hypothesis must be a testable prediction about the relationship, not a question or an aim.

points.title: Investigation methodologies
points.detail: Case study, classification and identification, experiment, fieldwork, literature review, modelling, product/process/system development, simulation. Be able to name the right one for a described investigation and justify it.

questions.q: A student measures the extension of a spring for a range of applied loads to find the spring constant. The methodology used is best described as
answer: B — a controlled experiment.
The independent variable (load) is deliberately manipulated and the dependent variable measured.
A correlational study looks for a relationship without manipulating anything.

card.title: Investigation methodologies
card.front: Name the methodologies and pick the right one for a described investigation.
back: Controlled experiment — manipulate an IV, measure a DV
Correlational study — look for a relationship without manipulating anything
Modelling and simulation — represent a system you can't test directly
Fieldwork, case study, classification and identification
Literature review, product/process/system development
Justify by what the investigation actually does, not what it's about

points.title: Generating and recording data
points.detail: Primary vs secondary data, qualitative vs quantitative, the logbook as authentication, and organising results into tables and graphs that follow the conventions.

questions.q: Distinguish primary from secondary data and explain the role of the logbook in a VCE physics investigation.
answer: Primary data is generated by the student through their own measurements.
Secondary data is obtained from another source — published results, databases, textbooks.
The logbook records measurements as they are taken, with dates and conditions.
It authenticates the data as the student's own work and provides a record for evaluating the method.

points.title: Measurement terms
points.detail: True value, uncertainty, accuracy, precision, repeatability, reproducibility, resolution, validity. The study design defines each of these tightly and the exam tests the distinctions — especially accuracy vs precision, and repeatability vs reproducibility.

questions.q: A group's five measurements of g are 9.79, 9.80, 9.79, 9.81 and 9.80 m s⁻². The accepted value is 9.80. Comment on the accuracy and precision of the results, and define both terms.
answer: Accuracy: how close a measurement is to the true value. The mean is 9.798, so the results are accurate.
Precision: how close repeated measurements are to each other. The spread is 0.02, so they are precise.
These are independent — a set can be precise but inaccurate if a systematic error is present.
Repeatability refers to the same person and equipment; reproducibility to a different person or setup.

points.title: Errors and uncertainty
points.detail: Random error affects precision and shows as a spread; systematic error shifts every reading the same way and comes from the instrument, its calibration or the method (including parallax). Repeating readings reduces random error only. Mistakes are repeated correctly, not reported. Uncertainty as mean ± value, and as uncertainty bars on a graph.

questions.q: A student's five timing measurements are 2.31, 2.28, 2.33, 2.30 and 2.32 s. The stopwatch was later found to start 0.15 s late every time. Identify the type of error this represents, state its effect on accuracy and precision, and explain whether repeating the measurements would help.
answer: A systematic error — it shifts every reading by the same amount in the same direction.
Accuracy is affected: all readings are 0.15 s too low relative to the true value.
Precision is unaffected: the readings are still tightly clustered.
Repeating does not help — averaging reduces random error only. The instrument must be corrected or the offset subtracted.

card.title: Errors and uncertainty
card.front: Random vs systematic error — what fixes each?
back: Random error — scatter around the true value; affects PRECISION
Reduce it by repeating measurements and averaging
Systematic error — shifts every reading the same way; affects ACCURACY
Causes: mis-calibrated instrument, zero offset, parallax, flawed method
Repeating does NOT reduce systematic error
A mistake is not an error — it's excluded, not reported

points.title: Significant figures and graphing conventions
points.detail: The sig fig rules, including leading and trailing zeros. Axes labelled with units and powers of ten, independent variable horizontal, a smooth trend line, extrapolation shown dashed. Linearising a graph and saying what its gradient physically means.

questions.q: A student calculates 4.56 × 2.1 and writes 9.576. State the correct answer to the appropriate number of significant figures and explain the rule.
answer: 2.1 has two significant figures; 4.56 has three.
For multiplication, the answer carries the number of significant figures of the least precise value.
Correct answer: 9.6.
Reporting extra digits implies a precision the measurements do not support.

points.title: Outliers and data quality
points.detail: Identifying outliers and accounting for them rather than quietly dropping them, which is an ethical as well as a technical point. Recognising contradictory, provisional or incomplete data.

questions.q: In a set of eight readings, one value sits far from the trend line while the other seven cluster tightly. Explain what the student should do and why simply deleting the value is poor practice.
answer: Identify it as a possible outlier and check the logbook for a recorded cause — a misread scale, a disturbed setup, a transcription slip.
If a cause is found, exclude it and state the reason explicitly in the report.
If no cause is found, report it and discuss it rather than removing it.
Silently deleting inconvenient data is unethical and can hide a real effect.

points.title: Conclusions and their limitations
points.detail: Distinguishing evidence from opinion, judging how far the data supports or refutes the hypothesis, stating the limitations of a conclusion and what further evidence would be needed.

questions.q: A student concludes: 'The results prove that resistance always increases with temperature for all materials.' Identify two problems with this conclusion and write an improved version.
answer: 'Prove' overstates it — data supports or is consistent with a hypothesis, it does not prove it.
'All materials' extends beyond the range investigated; only the material tested can be commented on.
Improved: 'The data supports the hypothesis that the resistance of this wire increases with temperature over the range 20–80 °C.'

card.title: Conclusions and their limitations
card.front: What can a conclusion legitimately claim?
back: State whether the data supports or refutes the hypothesis — nothing more
No new information in a conclusion
Limitations: range tested, sample size, assumptions made, uncontrolled variables
Correlation in the data does not establish causation
Say what further evidence would be needed

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Motion in two dimensions
points.title: Newton's three laws in one and two dimensions
points.detail: Two or more coplanar forces acting along a straight line and in two dimensions. Resolving forces into components, force diagrams, and the 'force on A by B' convention. Normal force and friction as the readily observable forces.

questions.q: A 5.0 kg box sits on a horizontal surface and is pulled by a 30 N force at 40° above the horizontal. Calculate the horizontal and vertical components of the applied force and the normal force acting on the box. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².
answer: Horizontal component: 30 cos(40°) = 23.0 N.
Vertical component: 30 sin(40°) = 19.3 N, directed upward.
Weight = 5.0 × 9.8 = 49 N downward.
Normal force = 49 − 19.3 = 29.7 N — the upward pull reduces it below the weight.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Motion in two dimensions
points.title: Uniform circular motion in a horizontal plane
points.detail: Fnet = mv²/r applied to a vehicle on a flat circular road, a vehicle on a banked track, and an object on the end of a string. The key skill is identifying which force actually supplies the centripetal force in each case.

questions.q: A 900 kg car rounds a flat circular bend of radius 50 m at 15 m s⁻¹. Calculate the net force required and identify which force supplies it.
answer: = 202 500 / 50 = 4050 N, directed toward the centre of the bend.
Friction between the tyres and the road supplies the centripetal force.
If the required force exceeds the maximum friction available, the car skids outward.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Motion in two dimensions
points.title: Satellite motion as uniform circular motion
points.detail: Modelling natural and artificial satellites — moons, planets, orbiting spacecraft — as objects in uniform circular orbit.

questions.q: Explain why a satellite in a stable circular orbit is accelerating even though its speed is constant.
answer: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, and velocity is a vector.
The direction of motion changes continuously, so the velocity changes even at constant speed.
The acceleration is centripetal — directed toward the centre of the orbit.
Gravity provides the force producing this acceleration.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Motion in two dimensions
points.title: Circular motion in a vertical plane
points.detail: Newton's second law at the highest and lowest positions only. Apparent weight at the top and bottom of a loop, and the minimum speed to maintain contact at the top.

questions.q: A 0.50 kg ball on a string of length 1.2 m is swung in a vertical circle. At the highest point the ball travels at 4.0 m s⁻¹. Calculate the tension in the string at that point. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².
answer: At the top, both tension and weight point toward the centre (downward).
T + mg = mv²/r
T = 6.67 − 4.9 = 1.8 N (2 significant figures).

card.title: Circular motion in a vertical plane
card.front: Set up Newton's second law at the top and the bottom of a vertical loop.
back: Net force always points to the centre: Fnet = mv²/r
At the TOP, both weight and normal force point down: N + mg = mv²/r
At the BOTTOM, they oppose: N − mg = mv²/r, so N is largest here
Apparent weight is N, not mg — heaviest at the bottom, lightest at the top
Minimum speed to keep contact at the top is when N = 0, so v = √(gr)

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Motion in two dimensions
points.title: Projectile motion near Earth's surface
points.detail: Horizontal and vertical components treated independently — constant horizontal velocity, vertical acceleration g. Plus a qualitative description of how air resistance changes the trajectory, range and speed.

questions.q: A ball is launched horizontally at 12 m s⁻¹ from a 20 m high cliff. Calculate the time of flight and the horizontal range, ignoring air resistance. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².
answer: Horizontal velocity is constant: range = 12 × 2.02 = 24 m.
The components are independent — the horizontal speed does not affect the time of fall.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Motion in two dimensions
points.title: Conservation of energy and momentum
points.detail: Applied to isolated systems in one dimension, theoretically and practically.

questions.q: A 2.0 kg trolley moving at 3.0 m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary 4.0 kg trolley and they move off together. Calculate their common velocity and the kinetic energy lost.
answer: Momentum before = 2.0 × 3.0 = 6.0 kg m s⁻¹.
Kinetic energy lost = 6.0 J, converted to heat, sound and deformation.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Motion in two dimensions
points.title: Impulse in an isolated system
points.detail: FΔt = mΔv for collisions between objects moving in a straight line, and impulse as the area under a force–time graph. Typically applied to vehicle safety — crumple zones extend Δt to reduce the force.

questions.q: A 1200 kg car travelling at 15 m s⁻¹ strikes a barrier and stops in 0.40 s. Calculate the average force on the car, and explain how a crumple zone reduces this force.
answer: Impulse = Δp = mΔv = 1200 × 15 = 1.8 × 10⁴ kg m s⁻¹.
A crumple zone increases the collision time Δt.
Δp is fixed by the mass and speed, so a larger Δt gives a smaller average force.

card.title: Impulse in an isolated system
card.front: Define impulse and connect it to vehicle safety.
back: Impulse = FΔt = change in momentum = mΔv
Impulse is the area under a force–time graph
For a given collision, Δp is fixed by the masses and velocities
Extending Δt therefore reduces the peak force
Crumple zones, airbags and seatbelts all extend Δt
Momentum is conserved in every collision in an isolated system

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Motion in two dimensions
points.title: Work done by a force
points.detail: Work as force × distance moved in the direction of the net force, and as the area under a force–distance graph (one dimension only).

questions.q: A satellite moves in a uniform circular orbit. Explain, with reference to the definition of work, why the gravitational force does no work on the satellite.
answer: Work is the product of force and displacement in the direction of that force.
In uniform circular motion the gravitational force acts toward the centre.
The velocity, and so the displacement, is always tangential — perpendicular to the force.
There is no displacement component along the force, so zero work is done and the speed is constant.

card.title: Work done by a force
card.front: Define work and say when a force does none.
back: W = Fs, using the component of force along the displacement
Work is the area under a force–distance graph
A force perpendicular to the motion does zero work
That's why the centripetal force in circular motion does no work
Work done against gravity becomes gravitational potential energy
Measured in joules; it is a scalar

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Motion in two dimensions
points.title: Kinetic energy and collisions
points.detail: Ek = ½mv² at low speeds. Distinguishing elastic from inelastic collisions by whether kinetic energy is conserved — momentum is conserved in both.

questions.q: Explain the difference between an elastic and an inelastic collision, and state which quantity is conserved in both.
answer: In an elastic collision, total kinetic energy is conserved.
In an inelastic collision, some kinetic energy is converted to heat, sound or deformation.
Momentum is conserved in both, provided the system is isolated.
A perfectly inelastic collision is one where the objects move off together.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Motion in two dimensions
points.title: Elastic potential energy
points.detail: Area under a force–distance graph, and Es = ½kΔx² for ideal springs obeying Hooke's law.

questions.q: A spring obeying Hooke's law with k = 250 N m⁻¹ is compressed by 0.080 m. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored, and state how this appears on a force–distance graph.
answer: On a force–distance graph the stored energy is the area under the line.
For an ideal spring the graph is a straight line through the origin, so the area is a triangle.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Motion in two dimensions
points.title: Gravitational potential energy
points.detail: Eg = mgΔh near Earth's surface, or from the area under a force–distance graph, or the area under a field–distance graph multiplied by mass. Energy dissipated to the environment counts as heat, sound and deformation.

questions.q: A 60 kg student climbs stairs of vertical height 4.5 m. Calculate the gain in gravitational potential energy, and explain why the horizontal distance travelled is irrelevant. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².
answer: Gravity acts vertically, so only vertical displacement is in the direction of the force.
Horizontal movement is perpendicular to gravity and so involves no work against it.

points.title: The field model
points.detail: Describing gravitation, magnetism and electricity using a field model — how a field explains interaction without contact.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by a field in physics and why the field model is needed.
answer: A field is a region in which an object experiences a force without physical contact.
It assigns a force-per-unit-property at every point in space.
It is needed to explain action at a distance — gravity, magnetism and electrostatic interaction all act without touching.

card.title: The field model and comparing fields
card.front: Compare gravitational, electric and magnetic fields.
back: A field explains action at a distance without contact
Gravitational — always attractive, monopoles only, acts on mass
Electric — attractive or repulsive, monopoles exist, acts on charge
Magnetic — attractive or repulsive, NO monopoles, always a dipole
All three follow inverse square behaviour for point sources
Field lines show direction; spacing shows strength

points.title: Comparing gravitational, magnetic and electric fields
points.detail: Directions and shapes, attractive and repulsive fields, and the existence of dipoles and monopoles. Gravity only attracts; magnetic monopoles don't exist. This comparison is a standard exam question.

questions.q: Compare gravitational, electric and magnetic fields in terms of the property they act on, whether they can repel, and the existence of monopoles.
answer: Gravitational: acts on mass, only ever attractive, monopoles exist (a single mass).
Electric: acts on charge, attractive or repulsive, monopoles exist (a single charge).
Magnetic: acts on moving charge or magnetic material, attractive or repulsive, NO monopoles — always a dipole.
All three follow an inverse square relationship for point sources.

card.title: The field model and comparing fields
card.front: Compare gravitational, electric and magnetic fields.
back: A field explains action at a distance without contact
Gravitational — always attractive, monopoles only, acts on mass
Electric — attractive or repulsive, monopoles exist, acts on charge
Magnetic — attractive or repulsive, NO monopoles, always a dipole
All three follow inverse square behaviour for point sources
Field lines show direction; spacing shows strength

points.title: Fields about a point mass or charge
points.detail: Direction and shape of the field, the inverse square law for its magnitude, and the qualitative potential energy change when a mass or charge moves within it.

questions.q: A point charge +Q produces an electric field. At a distance r the field strength is E. Determine the field strength at 3r, and sketch the shape and direction of the field lines around the charge.
answer: E/9 — the field follows an inverse square law, so tripling r divides the field by 9.
Field lines are radial, pointing away from a positive charge.
Lines are closer together near the charge, showing the stronger field there.
Field lines never cross.

card.title: Fields about a point mass or charge
card.front: Sketch and describe the field around a point mass and a point charge.
back: Radial field lines — into a mass, out of a positive charge, into a negative one
Magnitude follows an inverse square law: g = GM/r², E = kQ/r²
Lines closer together = stronger field; they never cross
Moving a mass away from M increases gravitational PE
Moving a like charge closer increases electric PE

points.title: Magnetic fields from currents
points.detail: Shapes and directions of the fields produced by bar magnets and by current-carrying wires, loops and solenoids. The right-hand rules.

questions.q: A current flows vertically upward through a straight wire. Describe the shape and direction of the magnetic field produced, and name the rule used.
answer: Concentric circles in horizontal planes around the wire.
Viewed from above, the field circulates anticlockwise.
Right-hand grip rule: thumb points along conventional current, fingers curl in the direction of B.

card.title: Magnetic fields from currents
card.front: Draw the field around a wire, a loop and a solenoid, and give the hand rule.
back: Straight wire — concentric circles around the wire
Right-hand grip: thumb along conventional current, fingers curl the field
Loop — field lines concentrate through the centre of the loop
Solenoid — uniform field inside, like a bar magnet outside
Solenoid rule: fingers curl with the current, thumb points to the north end
Bar magnet — lines leave N, enter S, continue S to N inside the magnet

points.title: Classifying fields
points.detail: Identifying a field as static or changing, and as uniform or non-uniform.

questions.q: Classify each as uniform or non-uniform and as static or changing: the field between charged parallel plates connected to a steady supply; the field around a bar magnet; the field inside a solenoid carrying AC.
answer: Between parallel plates on a steady supply — uniform and static.
Around a bar magnet — non-uniform and static.
Inside a solenoid on AC — approximately uniform but changing.
Uniform means the same magnitude and direction throughout; static means unchanging in time.

points.title: Electric field and electric force
points.detail: E = kQ/r² and F = kq₁q₂/r² for point charges.

questions.q: Two point charges of +2.0 μC and −3.0 μC are held 0.20 m apart. Calculate the magnitude of the force between them and state whether it is attractive or repulsive. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².
answer: F = kq₁q₂/r²
Attractive — the charges are unlike.

card.title: Electric field and electric force
card.front: Give the two point-charge relationships and how they connect.
back: Field of a point charge: E = kQ/r²
Force between two point charges: F = kq₁q₂/r²
The two are linked by F = qE
Field direction is the force on a POSITIVE test charge
Like charges repel, unlike attract

points.title: Accelerating a charge in a uniform electric field
points.detail: Potential energy changes W = qV, the field between parallel plates E = V/d, and the force on a charge F = qE.

questions.q: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 500 V between parallel plates 0.020 m apart. Calculate the field strength between the plates and the speed of the electron on arrival. Take e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
answer: Work done W = qV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 500 = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁷ J.
All of this becomes kinetic energy: ½mv² = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁷

card.title: Accelerating a charge in a uniform field
card.front: Give the three relationships for parallel plates.
back: Uniform field between plates: E = V/d
Force on a charge in that field: F = qE
Work done accelerating it: W = qV, which becomes kinetic energy
So qV = ½mv² gives the exit speed
Field lines are straight, evenly spaced, from positive plate to negative

points.title: Magnetic force on a charged particle
points.detail: F = qvB where v and B are perpendicular or parallel, with direction from the right-hand rule. The radius of the circular path from qvB = mv²/r, for v much less than c.

questions.q: A proton enters a uniform magnetic field with its velocity perpendicular to the field. Explain why it follows a circular path at constant speed, and state how the radius would change if its speed were doubled.
answer: The magnetic force F = qvB is always perpendicular to the velocity.
A force perpendicular to motion changes direction but does no work, so the speed is constant.
That constant perpendicular force provides the centripetal force, giving a circular path.
r = mv/qB, so doubling v doubles the radius.

card.title: Magnetic force on a charged particle
card.front: When does a magnetic field exert a force, and what path results?
back: F = qvB when v is perpendicular to B
Zero force when v is parallel to B — no component across the field
Direction from the right-hand rule; reverse it for a negative charge
The force is always perpendicular to v, so speed never changes
Circular path with qvB = mv²/r, giving r = mv/qB
Valid for v much less than c

points.title: Gravitational field and gravitational force
points.detail: g = GM/r², Fg = Gm₁m₂/r², and Eg = mgΔh for potential energy changes in a uniform gravitational field.

questions.q: Calculate the gravitational field strength at the surface of a planet of mass 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.4 × 10⁶ m. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
answer: g = GM/r²
g = 9.8 N kg⁻¹ (or m s⁻²).

card.title: Gravity, normal force and apparent weight
card.front: Distinguish weight from apparent weight, and explain orbital 'weightlessness'.
back: Field strength g = GM/r²; force Fg = Gm₁m₂/r²
Near the surface, PE change = mgΔh in a uniform field
Weight is the gravitational force; apparent weight is the normal force N
In orbit gravity is the only force, so N = 0 and apparent weight is zero
The astronaut is NOT weightless — gravity is what holds the orbit
They are in continuous free fall around the Earth

points.title: Gravitational potential energy from graphs
points.detail: The change in gravitational potential energy as the area under a force vs distance graph, and as the area under a field vs distance graph multiplied by mass.

questions.q: A graph of gravitational field strength against distance is given for a planet. Explain how to obtain the change in gravitational potential energy of a 500 kg satellite moving between two altitudes.
answer: Find the area under the field–distance graph between the two distances.
That area gives the energy change per unit mass.
Multiply by the mass: ΔEg = area × 500.
Equivalently, the area under a force–distance graph gives the energy change directly.

points.title: Force due to gravity and normal force
points.detail: Applying Fg and FN, including to satellites in orbit where the orbit is assumed uniform and circular. Apparent weight, and why an orbiting astronaut is not weightless.

questions.q: An astronaut aboard a space station in low Earth orbit appears to float. Explain why the astronaut is not weightless, using the terms weight and apparent weight.
answer: Weight is the gravitational force, which is still substantial in low Earth orbit — it is what keeps the station in orbit.
Apparent weight is the normal force from the surroundings.
In orbit gravity is the only force acting, so there is no normal force and apparent weight is zero.
The astronaut and station are both in continuous free fall around the Earth.

card.title: Gravity, normal force and apparent weight
card.front: Distinguish weight from apparent weight, and explain orbital 'weightlessness'.
back: Field strength g = GM/r²; force Fg = Gm₁m₂/r²
Near the surface, PE change = mgΔh in a uniform field
Weight is the gravitational force; apparent weight is the normal force N
In orbit gravity is the only force, so N = 0 and apparent weight is zero
The astronaut is NOT weightless — gravity is what holds the orbit
They are in continuous free fall around the Earth

points.title: Modelling satellite motion
points.detail: a = v²/r = 4π²r/T² for artificial satellites, the Moon and planets. Relating period to orbital radius, and geostationary orbits.

questions.q: A satellite orbits at radius 8.0 × 10⁶ m with a period of 7200 s. Calculate its orbital speed and centripetal acceleration.
answer: Circumference = 2πr = 2π × 8.0 × 10⁶ = 5.03 × 10⁷ m.
a = 6.1 m s⁻². Alternatively a = 4π²r/T² gives the same result.

points.title: Interaction of two fields
points.detail: Electric charges, magnetic poles and current-carrying conductors can attract or repel; masses only ever attract.

questions.q: Two long parallel wires carry current in the same direction. State whether they attract or repel and explain using the field of one wire acting on the other.
answer: They attract.
The first wire's magnetic field at the position of the second is perpendicular to that second current.
Applying the right-hand rule to F = nIlB gives a force directed toward the first wire, and the same applies in reverse.

card.title: Interaction of two fields
card.front: Which interactions attract, which repel?
back: Masses only ever attract
Like charges repel, unlike charges attract
Like magnetic poles repel, unlike attract
Parallel currents in the same direction attract; opposite directions repel
A field alone does nothing — it needs a second object to act on

points.title: Force on a current-carrying conductor
points.detail: F = nIlB, where the directions of I and B are perpendicular or parallel to each other.

questions.q: A wire of length 0.25 m carrying 3.0 A sits perpendicular to a 0.40 T magnetic field. Calculate the force on it, and state what happens if the wire is rotated to lie parallel to the field.
answer: Parallel to the field, there is no component of current perpendicular to B.
The force becomes zero.

points.title: Simple DC motors
points.detail: A single coil of several loops free to rotate about an axis in a uniform magnetic field, including the role of the split ring commutator in reversing the current each half turn.

questions.q: Explain the function of the split ring commutator in a simple DC motor, and state what would happen to the coil's motion without it.
answer: It reverses the direction of current through the coil every half turn.
This keeps the torque acting in the same rotational direction as the coil passes the vertical.
Without it, the torque would reverse after half a turn and the coil would oscillate rather than rotate continuously.

card.title: DC motors and torque
card.front: How does a simple DC motor work, and what increases its torque?
back: A current-carrying coil sits in an external magnetic field
Force on each side: F = nIlB, in opposite directions on opposite sides
That force pair creates a torque and the coil rotates
The split ring commutator reverses current each half turn to keep it turning one way
Torque increases with larger current, stronger external field, more loops
Torque is zero when the coil plane is perpendicular to the field

points.title: Torque in a simple motor
points.detail: The qualitative effect of the current, the strength of the external magnetic field and the number of loops of wire on the torque produced.

questions.q: State two changes that would increase the torque produced by a simple DC motor, and identify the coil orientation at which the torque is zero.
answer: Any two of: increase the current, increase the external magnetic field strength, increase the number of loops, increase the coil area.
Torque is zero when the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field.
At that point the forces on the sides act along the same line and produce no turning effect.

card.title: DC motors and torque
card.front: How does a simple DC motor work, and what increases its torque?
back: A current-carrying coil sits in an external magnetic field
Force on each side: F = nIlB, in opposite directions on opposite sides
That force pair creates a torque and the coil rotates
The split ring commutator reverses current each half turn to keep it turning one way
Torque increases with larger current, stronger external field, more loops
Torque is zero when the coil plane is perpendicular to the field

points.title: Particle accelerators
points.detail: Modelling acceleration of particles, limited to linear acceleration by a uniform electric field and direction change by a uniform magnetic field.

questions.q: In a particle accelerator, explain the role of the electric field and of the magnetic field, and why only one of them changes the particle's speed.
answer: A uniform electric field accelerates the charged particle, doing work on it and increasing its speed.
A magnetic field changes the direction of motion, steering the particle around the ring.
The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work.
Speed is therefore changed only by the electric field.

points.title: Magnetic flux
points.detail: Φ = B⊥A when the field is perpendicular to the area, plus a qualitative description of what happens at other angles between the area and the field.

questions.q: A square coil of side 0.15 m sits with its plane perpendicular to a uniform 0.40 T magnetic field. Calculate the magnetic flux through the coil, then state the flux when the coil is rotated so its plane is parallel to the field.
answer: With the plane parallel to the field, no field lines pass through the coil, so Φ = 0.

card.title: Magnetic flux and induced emf
card.front: State the flux and induction relationships, and explain the minus sign.
back: Flux Φ = B⊥A when the field is perpendicular to the area, in webers
Rotating the loop changes the perpendicular component and so changes Φ
Induced emf ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt
Bigger emf from a faster change, a bigger flux change, or more loops
The minus sign is Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change causing it
Lenz's law is conservation of energy — otherwise you'd get free energy

points.title: Induced emf
points.detail: ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt, with reference to the rate of change of flux, the number of loops the flux passes through, and the direction of the induced emf. The minus sign is Lenz's law — be able to explain it, not just quote it.

questions.q: A 50-turn coil experiences a change in flux from 8.0 × 10⁻³ Wb to 2.0 × 10⁻³ Wb in 0.030 s. Calculate the magnitude of the average induced emf, and explain the significance of the negative sign in ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt.
answer: The negative sign represents Lenz's law: the induced emf drives a current whose magnetic field opposes the change producing it.
This is a consequence of conservation of energy — otherwise the induced effect would reinforce the change and create energy from nothing.

card.title: Magnetic flux and induced emf
card.front: State the flux and induction relationships, and explain the minus sign.
back: Flux Φ = B⊥A when the field is perpendicular to the area, in webers
Rotating the loop changes the perpendicular component and so changes Φ
Induced emf ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt
Bigger emf from a faster change, a bigger flux change, or more loops
The minus sign is Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change causing it
Lenz's law is conservation of energy — otherwise you'd get free energy

points.title: DC generators and alternators
points.detail: Production of DC voltage using a split ring commutator, and AC voltage using slip rings. Know the shape of the output voltage in each case.

questions.q: A single coil rotates at constant frequency in a uniform magnetic field. Describe how the output differs when the coil is connected through slip rings compared with a split ring commutator.
answer: Slip rings: each end of the coil stays connected to its own ring, so the output is sinusoidal AC.
Split ring commutator: connections swap every half turn, flipping the negative half-cycles positive.
Peak emf is identical in both cases — only the external connection differs.
The DC output is pulsating, not constant.

card.title: DC generators and alternators
card.front: How do the two differ, and what does each output look like?
back: Both: a coil rotating in a magnetic field induces an emf
Alternator uses slip rings — each end of the coil stays on its own ring
Output is sinusoidal AC, reversing every half turn
DC generator uses a split ring commutator that swaps connections each half turn
Output is the same sine wave with the negative humps flipped positive
Peak emf is identical; only the connection to the external circuit differs

points.title: Photovoltaic cells
points.detail: Producing electricity from photovoltaic cells and why an inverter is needed to convert DC to AC for household use. Semiconductor action and inverter circuitry are not required.

questions.q: A household rooftop solar installation includes photovoltaic cells and an inverter. State the function of each.
answer: The photovoltaic cells convert light energy directly into DC electricity.
The inverter converts that DC into mains-frequency AC for household appliances and the grid.
Semiconductor action and inverter circuitry are not required knowledge.

card.title: Photovoltaic cells
card.front: How is household electricity produced from solar panels?
back: A photovoltaic cell converts light directly into DC electricity
Semiconductor action is NOT required — don't lose time on it
Household appliances and the grid run on AC
An inverter converts the DC output into mains-frequency AC
Inverter circuitry is also not required

points.title: Sinusoidal AC from a rotating loop
points.detail: Comparing AC voltages produced by uniform rotation of a loop in a constant magnetic field: frequency, period, amplitude, peak-to-peak voltage and peak-to-peak current.

questions.q: A coil rotating uniformly in a constant magnetic field produces a sinusoidal emf with a peak value of 12 V and a period of 20 ms. State the frequency, the peak-to-peak voltage, and the coil orientation at which the emf is maximum.
answer: Peak-to-peak = 2 × 12 = 24 V.
emf is maximum when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field.
At that orientation the flux is zero but changing at its fastest rate.

card.title: Sinusoidal AC from a rotating loop
card.front: Describe the output of a rotating loop and define its measures.
back: Uniform rotation in a constant field gives a sine wave emf
Period T is the time for one full rotation; frequency f = 1/T
Amplitude = peak voltage; peak-to-peak = twice that
emf is maximum when the coil plane is parallel to the field (flux changing fastest)
emf is zero when the coil plane is perpendicular (flux at a maximum)

points.title: RMS values
points.detail: The root-mean-square voltage as the constant DC voltage that would deliver the same power in a resistive component.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by the rms voltage of an AC supply, and why it is the value quoted for mains electricity.
answer: The rms voltage is the constant DC voltage that would deliver the same power to a resistive component.
It is the value that determines heating and power, not the instantaneous or peak value.
Quoting the peak would overstate the power delivered.
Australian mains is quoted as 230 V rms.

points.title: Converting between rms, peak and peak-to-peak
points.detail: Converting confidently in both directions for voltage and current, and picking the right one for a power calculation.

questions.q: An AC supply has a peak voltage of 340 V. Calculate the rms voltage and the peak-to-peak voltage.
answer: Peak-to-peak = 2 × Vpeak = 680 V.
Check which value a question gives you — mixing rms and peak is the most common error here.

points.title: Transformer action
points.detail: N₁/N₂ = V₁/V₂ = I₂/I₁ for an ideal transformer, explained through electromagnetic induction. Also why a transformer only works on AC.

questions.q: An ideal transformer has 200 turns on the primary and 50 on the secondary. The primary is supplied with 240 V AC drawing 2.0 A. Calculate the secondary voltage and current, and explain why the transformer would not operate on DC.
answer: I₂ = I₁ × N₁/N₂ = 2.0 × 200/50 = 8.0 A (power is conserved: 480 W both sides).
A transformer needs a CHANGING flux in the core to induce an emf in the secondary.
DC produces a constant current and so a constant flux — no change, no induced emf.

card.title: Transformer action
card.front: State the transformer relationship and explain why it needs AC.
back: N₁/N₂ = V₁/V₂ = I₂/I₁ for an ideal transformer
Power in equals power out when ideal, so raising V lowers I
Primary coil's changing current makes a changing flux in the core
That changing flux induces an emf in the secondary
DC gives constant flux, so no change, so no induced emf
Step-up has more turns on the secondary

points.title: Transmission losses
points.detail: Analysing the supply of power with losses across transmission lines, and why stepping voltage up for transmission reduces the power lost.

questions.q: A generator supplies 30 kW to transmission lines of total resistance 2.0 Ω. Compare the power lost when transmitted at 1000 V with the loss at 10 000 V, and explain the result.
answer: Power loss depends on I²R, so it depends on the CURRENT, not the supply voltage.
Raising the transmission voltage by 10 reduces the current by 10 and the loss by 100.

card.title: Transmission losses
card.front: Why is power transmitted at high voltage?
back: Power lost in the lines is Ploss = I²R — it depends on CURRENT, not supply voltage
Transformers step voltage up so the same power travels at lower current
Halving the current quarters the loss
Voltage drop across the lines is Vdrop = IR
Voltage delivered = supply voltage − voltage drop
Stepped back down near the consumer for safety

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: Light as a transverse electromagnetic wave
points.detail: Produced by the acceleration of charges, which creates changing electric fields and associated changing magnetic fields.

questions.q: Describe how an electromagnetic wave is produced and explain why it is classified as transverse.
answer: An accelerating charge produces a changing electric field.
That changing electric field generates an associated changing magnetic field, and the process self-propagates.
The electric and magnetic fields oscillate perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel.
Because the oscillation is perpendicular to propagation, the wave is transverse.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: All electromagnetic waves travel at c
points.detail: The same speed in a vacuum regardless of frequency or wavelength.

questions.q: A radio wave and a gamma ray both travel through a vacuum. Compare their speeds and their wavelengths.
answer: Both travel at exactly c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in a vacuum, regardless of frequency.
The radio wave has a far longer wavelength and lower frequency.
Since c = fλ is fixed, higher frequency necessarily means shorter wavelength.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: Standing waves
points.detail: Formation by superposition of a travelling wave and its reflection. Analysis is limited to standing waves with nodes at both ends — nodes, antinodes, and wavelength in terms of length.

questions.q: A string 1.2 m long is fixed at both ends and vibrates in its third harmonic. Calculate the wavelength and state the number of nodes and antinodes.
answer: For the nth harmonic with nodes at both ends, L = nλ/2.
The third harmonic has 4 nodes (including both ends) and 3 antinodes.
Standing waves form from superposition of a travelling wave and its reflection.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: Diffraction
points.detail: The directional spread of waves depends on the λ/w ratio — gap width or obstacle size relative to wavelength. Applied to the limits of imaging using electromagnetic waves.

questions.q: Explain why sound diffracts noticeably around a doorway but visible light does not.
answer: The amount of diffraction depends on the ratio λ/w — wavelength compared with the gap width.
Audible sound has wavelengths comparable to a doorway (around a metre), so λ/w is large and spreading is significant.
Visible light has wavelengths around 5 × 10⁻⁷ m, so λ/w is tiny and the spreading is negligible.

card.title: Diffraction
card.front: What determines how much a wave spreads?
back: Spreading depends on the ratio λ/w — wavelength to gap or obstacle size
Larger λ/w means more diffraction
Significant spreading when the gap is comparable to the wavelength
Long wavelengths diffract around obstacles; short ones cast sharper shadows
Sets the resolution limit when imaging with electromagnetic waves

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: Young's double slit experiment
points.detail: Evidence for the wave-like nature of light. Constructive interference at path differences of nλ and destructive at (n − ½)λ, for coherent waves.

questions.q: In a double slit experiment, light of wavelength 600 nm produces a pattern on a distant screen. State the path difference at the second bright fringe from the centre and at the first dark fringe, and explain why the pattern is evidence for a wave model.
answer: Second bright fringe: path difference = 2λ = 1.2 × 10⁻⁶ m.
First dark fringe: path difference = ½λ = 3.0 × 10⁻⁷ m.
Dark fringes require destructive interference — two contributions cancelling.
A particle model cannot explain how opening a second slit produces regions of darkness.

card.title: Young's double slit and fringe spacing
card.front: Give the path difference conditions and the spacing relationship.
back: Two coherent sources produce an interference pattern — evidence for waves
Constructive (bright): path difference = nλ
Destructive (dark): path difference = (n − ½)λ
Fringe spacing Δx = λL/d, valid when L is much greater than d
Longer λ or bigger L widens the fringes; wider slit separation narrows them
A particle model cannot produce dark fringes from two open slits

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: Interference pattern spacing
points.detail: Δx = λL/d when L is much greater than d, and the effect of changing wavelength, screen distance or slit separation on the fringe pattern.

questions.q: Two slits 0.25 mm apart are illuminated with 640 nm light. The screen is 2.0 m away. Calculate the fringe spacing, and state what happens to the spacing if the slit separation is halved.
answer: Halving d doubles Δx, so the fringes spread to about 10.2 mm apart.
Δx is inversely proportional to the slit separation.

card.title: Young's double slit and fringe spacing
card.front: Give the path difference conditions and the spacing relationship.
back: Two coherent sources produce an interference pattern — evidence for waves
Constructive (bright): path difference = nλ
Destructive (dark): path difference = (n − ½)λ
Fringe spacing Δx = λL/d, valid when L is much greater than d
Longer λ or bigger L widens the fringes; wider slit separation narrows them
A particle model cannot produce dark fringes from two open slits

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: Quantised photon energy
points.detail: E = hf = hc/λ, working in both joules and electron-volts and converting between them.

questions.q: Calculate the energy of a photon of wavelength 450 nm in both joules and electron-volts. Take hc = 1.99 × 10⁻²⁵ J m and 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
answer: Check which unit the question wants — energy level diagrams are usually in eV.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: The photoelectric effect
points.detail: Evidence for the particle-like nature of light. Reading graphs of photocurrent vs electrode potential and of kinetic energy vs frequency; Ek max = hf − φ; work function and threshold frequency; and the effect of the intensity of the incident light on the number of photoelectrons.

questions.q: Light of frequency 8.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz falls on a metal of work function 2.0 eV. Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons in eV, and state what happens to this value if the light intensity is doubled. Take h = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV s.
answer: Doubling the intensity does NOT change Ek(max).
It doubles the number of photons per second, so more photoelectrons and a larger photocurrent — but each still arrives with the same maximum energy.

questions.q: On a graph of maximum kinetic energy against frequency for the photoelectric effect, state the physical meaning of the gradient, the horizontal intercept and the vertical intercept.
answer: Gradient = Planck's constant h.
Horizontal intercept = the threshold frequency f₀, below which no emission occurs.
Vertical intercept = −φ, the negative of the work function.
The gradient is the same for every metal; only the intercepts shift.

card.title: The photoelectric effect
card.front: What are the four results, and which defeat the wave model?
back: Ek(max) = hf − φ, where φ is the work function
Below the threshold frequency f₀ = φ/h, NO electrons at any intensity
Ek(max) depends on frequency only, never on intensity
Intensity changes the NUMBER of photoelectrons, so the photocurrent
Emission is immediate — no time delay to accumulate energy
On an Ek vs f graph: gradient = h, x-intercept = f₀, y-intercept = −φ

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: Limitations of the wave model of light
points.detail: Which specific photoelectric results the wave model fails to explain — the threshold frequency, the absence of a time delay, and why intensity changes current but not maximum kinetic energy.

questions.q: State two experimental results of the photoelectric effect that the wave model of light cannot explain, and explain why the wave model fails in each case.
answer: The threshold frequency: below f₀ no electrons are emitted at any intensity.
A wave model predicts that sufficient intensity would eventually supply enough energy regardless of frequency.
The absence of a time delay: emission is immediate even at very low intensity.
A wave model predicts a measurable delay while energy accumulates in the metal.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: Electron diffraction
points.detail: Interpreting electron diffraction patterns as evidence for the wave-like nature of matter.

questions.q: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron travelling at 2.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹, and explain why a cricket ball does not show observable diffraction. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
answer: This is comparable to atomic spacing in a crystal, so diffraction is observable.
A cricket ball has a far larger momentum, giving λ around 10⁻³⁴ m — vastly smaller than any gap, so λ/w is effectively zero.

card.title: Electron diffraction
card.front: What does electron diffraction show, and what is the calculation?
back: Electrons fired at a crystal produce a diffraction pattern
Diffraction is a wave behaviour, so matter has wave properties
de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p = h/mv
Everyday objects have λ far too small to show diffraction
Matching a photon pattern means matching the wavelength

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: Photon vs electron diffraction patterns
points.detail: Distinguishing the patterns produced by photons from those produced by electrons.

questions.q: An electron beam and a beam of X-ray photons are directed at the same crystal, producing indistinguishable diffraction patterns. Explain what this tells you about the two beams.
answer: The diffraction pattern depends only on the wavelength relative to the crystal spacing.
Identical patterns therefore mean the two beams have the same wavelength.
For the electrons this is the de Broglie wavelength, λ = h/p.
It does NOT mean they have the same energy or momentum value in the same sense — only matching λ.

card.title: Photon vs electron diffraction patterns
card.front: Why do photon and electron diffraction patterns look the same?
back: Both produce identical concentric ring patterns through a crystal or aperture
The pattern depends only on the wavelength relative to the gap or spacing
For an electron the wavelength is the de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p
Matching patterns means matching wavelengths, not matching energies
This is the evidence that matter has wave-like properties
Given a pattern alone you cannot tell which particle made it

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: de Broglie wavelength
points.detail: λ = h/p for matter, and what it implies about why wave behaviour isn't observed for everyday objects.

questions.q: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of a 0.15 kg ball travelling at 30 m s⁻¹, and comment on why its wave nature is not observed. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
answer: This is vastly smaller than any aperture or obstacle the ball could encounter.
λ/w is effectively zero, so no diffraction or interference is observable.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: The idea of quantisation
points.detail: Its importance in developing knowledge about light and in explaining the nature of atoms.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by quantisation, and use it to account for the discrete lines observed in an atomic emission spectrum.
answer: Quantisation means a quantity is restricted to discrete values rather than a continuous range.
Electrons in an atom may only occupy allowed energy states.
A transition emits a photon of energy exactly equal to the difference between two states.
Only certain differences exist, so only certain photon energies appear — discrete lines, not a continuous band.

card.title: The idea of quantisation
card.front: What does it mean to say something is quantised, and why does it matter?
back: Quantised = restricted to discrete values, not a continuous range
Photon energy comes in packets E = hf, not any amount you like
Electrons in an atom sit only in allowed energy states
A transition emits or absorbs exactly the energy difference between two states
That is why spectra are discrete lines rather than a continuous band
Quantisation is what classical wave physics could not explain

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: Momentum of photons and matter
points.detail: Comparing the momentum of photons and of matter of the same wavelength using p = h/λ.

questions.q: A photon and an electron have the same wavelength of 5.0 × 10⁻¹¹ m. Compare their momentum and explain your reasoning.
answer: For both, p = h/λ — the relationship applies to photons and to matter.
Their momentum is identical, because momentum depends only on wavelength.
Their energies differ: the photon uses E = hc/λ while the electron uses its kinetic energy.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: Absorption and emission line spectra
points.detail: How atomic absorption and emission line spectra are produced, including those from metal vapour lamps.

questions.q: Explain how an absorption spectrum is produced and why the dark lines appear at the same wavelengths as the bright lines in that element's emission spectrum.
answer: White light passes through a cool gas; photons matching an allowed energy gap are absorbed, exciting electrons.
Those wavelengths are removed from the transmitted light, leaving dark lines.
The same energy gaps govern both absorption and emission for a given element.
So the absorbed and emitted photon energies, and therefore wavelengths, are identical.

card.title: Spectra and interpreting them
card.front: How are line spectra produced and how do you read one?
back: Emission — an excited electron drops down, emitting a photon of exactly ΔE
Absorption — a photon of exactly ΔE is absorbed, leaving a dark line
Same element gives the same line positions in both
Only discrete lines appear because energy states are quantised
Photon energy from the line: E = hf = hc/λ
Work in eV where the energy level diagram uses eV

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: Interpreting spectra
points.detail: Calculating the energy of an absorbed or emitted photon from spectral data using E = hf = hc/λ.

questions.q: An atom emits a photon when an electron falls from an energy state of −3.4 eV to one of −13.6 eV. Calculate the photon's energy in eV and its wavelength. Take hc = 1.24 × 10³ eV nm.
answer: This lies in the ultraviolet.

card.title: Spectra and interpreting them
card.front: How are line spectra produced and how do you read one?
back: Emission — an excited electron drops down, emitting a photon of exactly ΔE
Absorption — a photon of exactly ΔE is absorbed, leaving a dark line
Same element gives the same line positions in both
Only discrete lines appear because energy states are quantised
Photon energy from the line: E = hf = hc/λ
Work in eV where the energy level diagram uses eV

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: Photon emission and electron energy states
points.detail: Emission or absorption of a photon as a change in the electron energy state of an atom, with the difference between the states equal to the photon energy.

questions.q: An atom has energy levels at −10.0 eV, −6.0 eV and −2.5 eV. A photon of 3.0 eV is directed at the atom in its ground state. Explain whether it will be absorbed.
answer: The available transitions from the ground state require 4.0 eV or 7.5 eV.
A 3.0 eV photon matches no energy gap.
It is not absorbed and passes through — absorption is all-or-nothing, not partial.

card.title: Photon emission and electron energy states
card.front: Link a transition on an energy level diagram to a photon.
back: Electrons occupy discrete energy levels, most negative at the ground state
A transition between two levels emits or absorbs exactly the difference
Ephoton = E(higher) − E(lower), so λ = hc/ΔE
Bigger energy gap means higher frequency and shorter wavelength
An atom can only absorb a photon that exactly matches a gap

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: The single photon or electron double slit experiment
points.detail: Interpreting it as evidence for the dual nature of both light and matter.

questions.q: In a double slit experiment, photons are fired one at a time over several hours. Describe what is observed and explain why the result is significant.
answer: Each photon arrives as a single localised dot on the detector — particle-like behaviour.
Over time the accumulated dots build up the interference pattern — wave-like behaviour.
Each individual photon must therefore interfere with itself, passing through both slits.
This is evidence that light is neither purely wave nor purely particle, but exhibits both natures.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: Limitations of classical mechanics
points.detail: Where classical mechanics breaks down for motion approaching the speed of light.

questions.q: Explain why classical mechanics fails for objects moving close to the speed of light, giving one specific prediction it gets wrong.
answer: Classical mechanics assumes time and length are absolute and velocities add simply.
It predicts that continued acceleration would carry an object past the speed of light.
Relativity shows kinetic energy is (γ − 1)mc², which diverges as v approaches c.
Infinite energy would be required, so a massive object can never reach c.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: Einstein's two postulates
points.detail: The laws of physics are the same in all inertial (non-accelerated) frames of reference, and the speed of light is constant for all observers regardless of the motion of observer or source.

questions.q: State Einstein's two postulates of special relativity.
answer: The laws of physics are the same in all inertial (non-accelerating) frames of reference.
The speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all observers, regardless of the motion of the source or observer.
The second postulate is the one that forces time dilation and length contraction.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: The Michelson–Morley experiment
points.detail: Interpreting its null result as evidence supporting the special theory of relativity.

questions.q: Describe what the Michelson–Morley experiment set out to detect, what result it obtained, and how that result supports special relativity.
answer: It aimed to detect Earth's motion through the hypothetical luminiferous aether.
It compared light travelling along two perpendicular arms, expecting a shift in the interference fringes.
No shift was observed — a null result.
This is consistent with Einstein's second postulate: the speed of light is the same for all observers regardless of motion.

card.title: The Michelson–Morley experiment
card.front: What was it looking for, what did it find, and why does it matter?
back: It was designed to detect Earth's motion through the luminiferous aether
It compared light travelling along two perpendicular arms
Expected a shift in the interference fringes; found none — a null result
No evidence for an aether, and no dependence of light speed on motion
Supports Einstein's second postulate: c is the same for all observers

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: Special relativity vs classical physics
points.detail: Comparing Einstein's theory with the principles of classical physics, including what each predicts about adding velocities.

questions.q: A spacecraft travelling at 0.7c fires a projectile forward at 0.5c relative to itself. State what classical physics predicts for the projectile's speed relative to Earth, and what relativity says.
answer: Classical physics predicts simple addition: 0.7c + 0.5c = 1.2c.
Relativity forbids this — no object can exceed c in any frame.
The relativistic result is less than c, approaching but never reaching it.
Velocities do not add linearly at relativistic speeds.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: Proper time
points.detail: t₀ as the time interval between two events measured in the reference frame where the two events occur at the same point in space. Identifying which observer measures it is usually the hard part.

questions.q: A muon created in the upper atmosphere travels toward Earth at 0.98c. Its half-life measured at rest is 1.5 μs. Identify which observer measures proper time, and calculate the half-life as measured from Earth.
answer: Proper time is measured in the muon's frame, where creation and decay occur at the same point in space.
t = γt₀ = 5.03 × 1.5 = 7.5 μs as measured from Earth.
This dilation is why muons reach the surface in far greater numbers than classical physics predicts.

card.title: Proper time and proper length
card.front: Define both and identify which observer measures them.
back: Proper time t₀ — measured where the two events happen at the SAME PLACE
That's the observer travelling with the clock
Proper length L₀ — measured in the frame where the object is AT REST
Everyone else measures a longer time and a shorter length
t = γt₀ and L = L₀/γ, with γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²)
Time dilates, length contracts — identify the frame first, always

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: Proper length
points.detail: L₀ as the length measured in the reference frame in which the object is at rest.

questions.q: A spacecraft of rest length 80 m travels past an observer at 0.60c. Calculate the length measured by that observer, and state who measures the proper length.
answer: Proper length is measured in the frame where the object is at rest — an observer aboard the spacecraft.
Everyone else measures it shorter; length contracts while time dilates.

card.title: Proper time and proper length
card.front: Define both and identify which observer measures them.
back: Proper time t₀ — measured where the two events happen at the SAME PLACE
That's the observer travelling with the clock
Proper length L₀ — measured in the frame where the object is AT REST
Everyone else measures a longer time and a shorter length
t = γt₀ and L = L₀/γ, with γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²)
Time dilates, length contracts — identify the frame first, always

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: Time dilation and length contraction
points.detail: t = t₀γ and L = L₀/γ, with γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²). Knowing which frame measures which quantity, and that time dilates while length contracts.

questions.q: A spacecraft travels at 0.80c relative to Earth. Calculate γ, then find the time an Earth observer measures for a process taking 6.0 s aboard the spacecraft.
answer: The 6.0 s is proper time — the events occur at the same place aboard the craft.
t = γt₀ = 1.67 × 6.0 = 10 s as measured from Earth.
The Earth observer measures a longer time: the moving clock runs slow.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: Examples of special relativity
points.detail: Muons reaching Earth's surface despite their half-life, particle accelerator lengths accounting for relativistic effects, and corrections to GPS satellite time signals due to orbital velocity.

questions.q: Explain why GPS satellites require relativistic corrections to their time signals.
answer: The satellites move at high orbital speed relative to receivers on the ground.
Time dilation means their onboard clocks run slow relative to Earth clocks by a predictable amount.
GPS position is calculated from signal travel times, so a clock error becomes a position error.
Uncorrected, the error would accumulate to kilometres within a day.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: Mass–energy
points.detail: Etot = Ek + E0 = γmc², rest energy E0 = mc², and relativistic kinetic energy Ek = (γ − 1)mc².

questions.q: An electron is accelerated to 0.80c. Calculate its total energy as a multiple of its rest energy, and state its kinetic energy in the same terms.
answer: Etot = γmc² = 1.67 × E₀, so about 1.7 times the rest energy.
Ek = (γ − 1)mc² = 0.67 × E₀.
Note Ek is NOT ½mv² at this speed — the classical formula fails as v approaches c.

card.title: Mass–energy
card.front: Give the relativistic energy relationships.
back: Rest energy E₀ = mc²
Total energy Etot = γmc²
Kinetic energy Ek = (γ − 1)mc², NOT ½mv² at high speed
Etot = Ek + E₀
As v approaches c, γ diverges and energy grows without limit
Which is why a massive object can never reach c

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Light, matter and relativity
points.title: Mass converted to energy in the Sun
points.detail: How nuclear fusion converts matter to energy, decreasing the Sun's mass and emitting electromagnetic radiation.

questions.q: Explain how the Sun produces energy and what happens to its mass, referring to E = mc².
answer: Nuclear fusion joins hydrogen nuclei into helium in the core.
The mass of the products is slightly less than the mass of the reactants.
That mass difference is converted to energy according to E = mc², radiated as electromagnetic radiation.
The Sun's mass therefore decreases continuously, by roughly four million tonnes per second.

points.title: Physics concepts behind your investigation
points.detail: The concepts specific to your own investigation and why they matter — definitions of key terms, and the representations and conventions used to express them.

questions.q: Explain why a scientific poster must define the key physics concepts behind the investigation, and give an example for an investigation into projectile range.
answer: The reader must be able to follow the reasoning without prior knowledge of your particular setup.
Definitions establish the meaning of the terms used consistently through the poster.
Example: define range, launch angle, and the independence of horizontal and vertical components.
The concepts also justify why the chosen variables are the relevant ones.

points.title: Designing the investigation
points.detail: A testable question and hypothesis, and clear identification of the independent, dependent and controlled variables.

questions.q: A student investigates how the period of a pendulum depends on its length. Identify the independent, dependent and one controlled variable, and state one way to reduce random error in the timing.
answer: Independent variable: length of the pendulum.
Dependent variable: period of oscillation.
Controlled: mass of the bob, release angle, or location (so g is constant).
Time 10 oscillations and divide by 10, repeated several times, to reduce random timing error.

card.title: Designing the investigation
card.front: What must a good investigation design specify?
back: A question that can actually be answered by measurement
Independent, dependent and controlled variables identified explicitly
Methodology chosen and justified against the question
Equipment, procedure, the range of IV values and how many measurements
Repeat measurements to handle random error
Justify each choice — that's where the marks are

points.title: Methodology and method
points.detail: Choosing the appropriate methodology, then the equipment, procedure, range of values and number of measurements — and being able to justify each choice.

questions.q: Explain why a student investigating the relationship between two variables should take measurements across a wide range of the independent variable rather than a narrow one.
answer: A wide range makes any trend clearer relative to the scatter in the data.
It allows the form of the relationship to be identified — linear, inverse or square — rather than assumed.
A narrow range can make a curve look linear and support a wrong conclusion.

points.title: Safety and ethical guidelines
points.detail: Risk assessment informed by safety data sheets, relevant occupational health and safety guidance, and ethical conduct in carrying out and reporting the investigation.

questions.q: A student plans an investigation using a high-voltage power supply and a laser. Identify two specific safety considerations and one ethical consideration.
answer: Safety: never look directly into the laser beam or its reflection; use the lowest power that works.
Safety: isolate the high-voltage supply before altering the circuit, and use insulated leads.
Ethical: report all data honestly, including results that do not support the hypothesis.
A written risk assessment should be completed before practical work begins.

points.title: Generating and recording primary data
points.detail: Systematic recording in the logbook, replicate measurements, appropriate units and significant figures, and tables that follow the conventions.

questions.q: Describe three features of a well-constructed results table for a physics investigation.
answer: Column headings state the quantity and its unit, e.g. 'Time (s)'.
Values recorded to a consistent and appropriate number of significant figures, reflecting the instrument's resolution.
Repeat measurements shown individually, with a mean calculated in a separate column.
The independent variable is usually the first column, ordered systematically.

points.title: Analysing the data
points.detail: Processing data with the right relationships, graphing and linearising, interpreting the gradient, and identifying and accounting for outliers.

questions.q: A student obtains a curved graph of period against length for a pendulum. Explain how they could linearise it and what the gradient of the linearised graph would represent.
answer: The relationship is T = 2π√(L/g), so T is proportional to √L.
Plot T against √L, or plot T² against L.
T² against L gives a straight line through the origin with gradient 4π²/g.
g can then be found as 4π² divided by the gradient.

points.title: Evaluating the method
points.detail: Accuracy, precision, repeatability, reproducibility and validity of your measurements; identifying sources of random and systematic error and suggesting specific improvements.

questions.q: A student's experimental value for g is consistently 8.9 m s⁻² across all trials. Identify the likely type of error, suggest a plausible cause, and state one improvement.
answer: A systematic error — every trial is low by a similar amount, so the results are precise but inaccurate.
Plausible cause: air resistance, a consistently late stopwatch start, or a mis-measured drop height.
Improvement: use light gates instead of a manual stopwatch to remove reaction time.
Repeating more trials would not help, since averaging does not remove systematic error.

points.title: Conclusions and limitations
points.detail: Judging how far the evidence supports the hypothesis, stating the limitations of the conclusion, and suggesting further investigation — with no new information introduced in the conclusion.

questions.q: Distinguish between a limitation of an investigation and an error in it, and give one example of each for an experiment measuring the acceleration due to gravity by timing a falling object.
answer: A limitation is a constraint on what the investigation can conclude; an error is a fault in the measurement.
Limitation: only one object and one drop height were tested, so the conclusion cannot be generalised.
Error: reaction time in starting and stopping the stopwatch — a random error affecting precision.
Air resistance producing a consistently low value would be a systematic error.

card.title: Conclusions and limitations
card.front: How do you conclude a practical investigation?
back: Answer the question directly, referring to your own data
State how far the evidence supports the hypothesis
Name the limitations: range, sample size, uncontrolled variables, assumptions
Distinguish limitations from errors you could have avoided
Suggest a specific improvement or extension, not just 'be more careful'

points.title: The scientific poster
points.detail: The required sections, the 600-word limit excluding tables, graphs, captions and references, and the one-sentence communication statement at the centre occupying 20–25% of the poster.

questions.q: State the word limit for a VCE Physics scientific poster, what that limit excludes, and the required proportion of the poster occupied by the communication statement.
answer: 600 words.
Excludes tables, graphs, captions, acknowledgements and references.
The one-sentence communication statement sits centrally and occupies 20–25% of the poster area.

card.title: The scientific poster
card.front: What are the format requirements?
back: 600 word limit, excluding tables, graphs, captions and references
A one-sentence communication statement reporting the key finding
It sits in the centre and occupies 20–25% of the poster
Sections: title, introduction, methodology and method, results, discussion, conclusion
Acknowledgements and references included
Results shown as tables and graphs, not prose
